episodes.158332: Thunderstorms initiated during the mid afternoon hours on May 13th along a surface trough of low pressure, draped over the western Sandhills. As storms tracked southeast into more favorable moisture, they became severe with large hail and damaging winds. Hail up to 2 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 74 MPH were reported during the late afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.158378: During the evening hours of May 13th into the early morning hours of May 14th, thunderstorms developed in southwestern Nebraska due to a frontal boundary set up in eastern Colorado. These storms produced hail up to ping pong ball size along with damaging wind gusts up to 80 mph in the area.
episodes.158380: During the afternoon hours of May 13th, thunderstorms developed in east-central Colorado due to a frontal boundary set up in eastern Colorado. These storms produced hail up to nickel size that measured up to 1 inch in depth on the ground.
episodes.158384: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 13th, a thunderstorm moved through northwestern Kansas due to a frontal boundary set up in eastern Colorado. This storm produced a landspout and hail up to hen egg size.
episodes.158507: A cold frontal boundary slowly moved southward across the Lake Region of South FL. This in combination with abundant moisture, cloud erosion, and strengthening deep layer shear near 35-45 kts allowed for strong to severe storms to develop across the region, especially inland areas and the Lake Okeechobee Region. Strong winds and heavy rain were recorded, though hail was the main hazard.
episodes.164828: On the evening of May 12th an ice jam formed on the Buckland River approximately one quarter of a mile below the community of Buckland. This caused the river to backup and result in significant flooding in Buckland. The ice jam broke on May 14th and allowed floodwaters to recede. Local residents report this could be the worst flooding the village has seen since 1978.

events.narrative: Village officials reported that water levels rose rapidly in the community after the ice jam formed the evening of May 12th. Water and ice was overbank and inundating most of the community with road access to the airport and other locations cut off. By May 14th, water levels dropped significantly with vehicles now able to access to the airport. At the height of the flooding, most of the Buckland was inundated with floodwater up to five feet deep causing extensive damage to homes, evacuations, damage to water treatment facilities, eroded roads and building foundations, and a bulk fuel tank hazardous materials release. ||The Governor declared a state disaster for Buckland on May 19th.
